prompt:
You are a senior typographer and information designer. You lay out data tables for publication. You judge layouts by looking at the rendered result as a whole: what the table is for, how a reader scans and compares it, which columns belong together or play the same role, proportion and rhythm across columns, a clear hierarchy of headers and groups, whether rows read as units, whether words, numbers and identifiers stay intact, and how text and white space are distributed. Fewer lines or a shorter table is not automatically better, and neither is equal widths or symmetry; decide case by case and say why.

Table: Operating and Financial Metrics (language en).
Grid: 5 columns × 7 rows. Row headers: yes (first logical column identifies each row).
Per-column content facts (content px at 15px font, excluding padding):
  col 1: header "Metric" · longest unbreakable word 82px · one-line width 407px
  col 2: header "FY 2022" · longest unbreakable word 61px · one-line width 61px
  col 3: header "FY 2023" · longest unbreakable word 62px · one-line width 62px
  col 4: header "FY 2024" · longest unbreakable word 58px · one-line width 61px
  col 5: header "Q1 2025" · longest unbreakable word 63px · one-line width 63px
Each column also has 21px of padding+border, so a column given width w px shows w−21 px of text.
Available width: 360px (the dashed pink box). The column widths you choose must sum to at most 359px.
This table cannot fit without splitting words at 360px. You MAY choose a total wider than 359px (the reader then scrolls horizontally), or squeeze and accept splits — a design decision.
Fixed: content, font, 15px font size, padding, borders, colours, alignment. You control ONLY the column widths.

Your understanding so far: {"purpose":"A compact operating and financial KPI table for comparing six metrics across FY 2022, FY 2023, FY 2024 and Q1 2025; readers use it to scan trends over time rather than read prose.","reading":"Scan the first column down to find the metric, then read across the four period columns to compare values. The metric column is the row index; the four period columns form a matched numeric band. Long metric labels will wrap at word boundaries, and period headers can stack as FY / 2022 and Q1 / 2025, but digits and currency/percent tokens should not split.","groups":["Column 1: row-label/index column, separate from all values.","Columns 2–5: one peer group of period-value columns; equal width is appropriate because they play the same role and support across-row comparison. Q1 2025 is a shorter latest period but still belongs to this band."],"keep_intact":["Metric names' unbreakable words such as 'percentage', 'acquisition' and 'recurring' — no mid-word splits","Numeric values including $, commas, decimals and % (e.g. $1,800, 71.3%)","Year digits 2022, 2023, 2024, 2025 — headers may break only after 'FY' or 'Q1'"],"may_wrap":["Long metric labels at spaces or commas, over 2–4 lines","Period headers into two lines: FY / 2022, Q1 / 2025","Header rows and metric rows may grow taller; numeric body cells should stay on one line"]}

The first image is the one-line content overview. The other images are real browser renders of your current designs:
Design r1A: widths [103, 76, 76, 76, 76] · table 408×813px · row heights [60, 153, 83, 153, 106, 129, 129] · column headers wrapped 4/5 · tallest cell 6 lines · mid-word splits 5 · OVERFLOWS the box by 48px
Design r1B: widths [103, 80, 80, 80, 80] · table 424×813px · row heights [60, 153, 83, 153, 106, 129, 129] · column headers wrapped 4/5 · tallest cell 6 lines · mid-word splits 3 · OVERFLOWS the box by 64px
Design r1C: widths [103, 84, 84, 84, 84] · table 440×790px · row heights [36, 153, 83, 153, 106, 129, 129] · column headers wrapped 0/5 · tallest cell 6 lines · mid-word splits 0 · OVERFLOWS the box by 80px

Look carefully at each render as a whole and in detail. For each design say what works and what is visually wrong, and WHY it happens (which width causes it). Then propose up to 3 improved designs: refine the most promising, fix the problems you saw, and try a new idea if an important alternative is unexplored. If no design can be meaningfully improved, set "done": true and return no new designs.
Reply ONLY JSON: {"critique":[{"design":"name","good":"","problems":"","cause":""}],"done":false,"designs":[{"name":"short-name","widths":[int px],"change":"what you changed and why"}]}

log.raw: {"critique":[{"design":"r1A","good":"The four period columns are equal, which correctly signals that FY 2022–Q1 2025 are one peer group; the metric column is clearly separated as a row index. Row banding and borders read cleanly, so rows are easy to follow.","problems":"The table is 813px tall and each metric row is 3–6 lines, so the eye can no longer scan down the metric column or across a row. Values are broken mid-token ($318.4 / M, $548.1 / M, 121 / %), headers stack into 4–5 fragments (FY / 202 / 2), and the whole table is clipped 48px past the box.","cause":"The metric column is fixed at 103px (82px of text) — barely one unbreakable word — while the period columns get only 76px (55px of text), less than the 61–63px their values need. Both columns are too narrow for their content, so every cell wraps, inflating height and splitting numbers."},{"design":"r1B","good":"Equal 80px period columns keep the value band rhythmic, and a few more values now fit ($1,840, 71.3%, 38.2%), so some rows read at a glance.","problems":"Still 813px tall with 6-line metric rows; the widest values ($318.4M, $402.7M, $511.9M, $101.2M) still split and the Q1 2025 column is cut off at the right edge. The extra 4px per period column bought almost nothing visually.","cause":"80px gives 59px of text, still under the ~63px the money values need; meanwhile the metric column remains at 103px, so the dominant cause of the height — the 407px of label squeezed into 82px — was left untouched."},{"design":"r1C","good":"84px period columns are the first design that works for the numbers: every value stays on one line, headers read as single lines (FY 2022, Q1 2025), and there are no mid-word splits. The table drops to 790px and looks calm and regular.","problems":"The metric column still produces 6-line rows, so the table is nearly as tall as r1A; and because nothing was given to the labels, the width went entirely into the periods, pushing the table 80px out of the box — the Q1 2025 column is mostly clipped. Reading a row means horizontal scrolling before you can even see the value.","cause":"Spending all available width on the four period columns (4×84=336) while keeping the metric column at 103px fixes the values but leaves the real bottleneck (a 407px label column) unsolved, and 103+336=440 cannot fit in 360."}],"done":false,"designs":[{"name":"r2A-scroll-balanced","widths":[176,84,84,84,84],"change":"Accept horizontal scrolling deliberately: give the metric column 176px (155px of text, ~2–3 lines per label instead of 6) and lock the four period columns at 84px, the smallest width that keeps every value and header on one line. Total 512px. Table height should fall from ~813px to roughly 480px, and the row index becomes scannable again."},{"name":"r2B-label-first","widths":[224,84,84,84,84],"change":"Push the priority further toward the row index: 224px lets 'Net revenue retention, trailing twelve months' and 'Sales and marketing expense as a percentage of revenue' break into 2 lines, making the table read like a real index. Period columns stay at the proven 84px. Total 560px — more scroll, but the tallest cell drops to 2–3 lines and the table becomes genuinely readable across a row."},{"name":"r2C-min-overflow","widths":[150,86,86,86,86],"change":"Compromise for readers who dislike scrolling: keep the metric column as wide as the budget allows while numbers stay intact, and add 2px of slack to each period column (86px = 65px of text) so the money values have breathing room rather than touching the cell edge. Total 494px, the smallest overflow that still guarantees no split numbers and no clipped period headers."}]}
